{{Short description|Class of points in a function's domain defined by having the same image by that map}}
{{Use American English|date=March 2021}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=March 2021}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''fiber''' ([[American English|US English]]) or '''fibre''' ([[British English]]) of a [[map (mathematics)|map]] or [[function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f:X\to Y</math> is an equivalence class in ''X'' for the relation of having the same image under ''f''. If ''y'' is that image, then this fiber equals the [[inverse image]] <math>f^{-1}(y) = \{ x\in X : f(x) = y \}</math> of <math>y</math><ref name=leem2011/>{{rp|p.69}}
and is called the fiber of ''f'' over&nbsp;''y''.

==Properties and applications==

===In elementary set theory===

Any map <math>f:X\to Y</math> defines a relation <math>\equiv_f</math> on ''X'', where <math>x_1\equiv_f x_2</math> holds when <math>f(x_1)=f(x_2)</math>, and this is always an [[equivalence relation]]. The '''fibers of''' <math>f</math> are the [[equivalence classes]] for this relation&nbsp;<math>\equiv_f</math>. Each such fiber is associated to the (by definition constant) value of ''f'' on the fiber, and if <math>y\in Y</math> is that value (necessarily an element of the image set of ''f''), then the fiber is the set <math>f^{-1}(y) = \{ x\in X : f(x) = y\}</math> of [[preimage]]s of ''y'' under ''f'', which is called the fiber of ''f'' over ''y''. The set of all fibers of ''f'' forms is a [[partition (mathematics)|partition]] of <math>X</math>. The mentioned correspondence defines a [[bijection]] from the [[quotient set]] <math>X/{\equiv_f}</math> (the set of fibers of ''f'') to the image set <math>f(X)</math>.
Note that in case <math>f</math> is not a [[surjective map]], one only considers fibers over elements of the subset <math>f(X)</math> of ''Y'', thus avoiding the [[empty set]], which cannot be an element of any [[partition of a set|partition]],
among the fibers of ''f''. The fiber containing an element <math>x\in X</math> is the set <math>f^{-1}(f(x))</math>.

For example, let <math>f</math> be the function from <math>\R^2</math> to <math>\R</math> that sends point <math>(a,b)</math> to <math>a+b</math>. The fiber of 5 under <math>f</math> are all the points on the straight line with [[equation (mathematics)|equation]] <math>a+b=5</math>.  The fibers of <math>f</math> are that line and all the straight lines parallel to it, which form a partition of the plane <math>\R^2</math>.

More generally, if <math>f</math> is a [[linear map]] from some [[linear vector space]] <math>X</math> to some other linear space <math>Y</math>, the fibers of <math>f</math> are [[affine space|affine subspaces]] of <math>X</math>, which are all the translated copies of the [[null space]] of <math>f</math>.

If <math>f</math> is a [[real number|real]]-valued [[function of several real variables]], the fibers of the function are the [[level set]]s of <math>f</math>.  If <math>f</math> is also a [[continuous function]] and <math>y\in\R</math> is in the [[image (mathematics)|image]] of <math>f,</math> the level set <math>f^{-1}(y)</math>  will typically be a [[Curve (mathematics)|curve]] in [[Plane (mathematics)|2D]], a [[Surface (mathematics)|surface]] in [[Three-dimensional space|3D]], and, more generally, a [[hypersurface]] in the domain of <math>f.</math>

===In topology===

In [[point set topology]], one generally considers functions from [[topological spaces]] to topological spaces.

If <math>f</math> is a [[continuous function (topology)|continuous function]] and if <math>Y</math> (or more generally, the image set <math>f(X)</math>) is a [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]] then every fiber is a [[closed set|closed subset]] of <math>X.</math> In particular, if <math>f</math> is a [[local homeomorphism]] from <math>X</math> to <math>Y</math>, each fiber of <math>f</math> is a [[discrete space|discrete]] [[topological subspace|subspace]] of <math>X</math>. 

A function between topological spaces is called {{em|{{visible anchor|monotone}}}} if every fiber is a [[connected space|connected]] [[topological subspace|subspace]] of its domain. A function <math>f : \R \to \R</math> is monotone in this topological sense if and only if it is [[nonincreasing function|non-increasing]] or [[nondecreasing function|non-decreasing]], which is the usual meaning of "[[monotone function]]" in [[real analysis]]. 

A function between topological spaces is (sometimes) called a {{em|[[proper map]]}} if every fiber is a [[compact space|compact]] subspace of its domain. However, many authors use other non-equivalent competing definitions of "proper map" so it is advisable to always check how a particular author defines this term. A [[continuous function|continuous]] [[Closed map|closed]] [[surjective function]] whose fibers are all compact is called a {{em|[[perfect map]]}}.

A [[fiber bundle]] is a function <math>f</math> between [[topological spaces]] <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> whose fibers have certain special properties related to the topology of those spaces.

===In algebraic geometry===

In [[algebraic geometry]], if <math>f : X \to Y</math> is a [[morphism of schemes]], the '''fiber''' of a [[element (category theory)|point]] <math>p</math> in <math>Y</math> is the [[fiber product of schemes]] 
<math display=block>X \times_Y \operatorname{Spec} k(p)</math> 
where <math>k(p)</math> is the [[residue field]] at <math>p.</math>
